### Migration

The number of people immigrating to England and Wales from outside the UK decreased in the year to mid-2025, compared with the previous year. The number of people emigrating from England and Wales to outside the UK increased in the same period. This led to an overall decrease in net international migration compared with the previous year.

We estimate that in the year to mid-2025:

*   816,500 people immigrated to England and Wales from outside the UK (down from 1,197,500 in the year to mid-2024)

*   604,800 people emigrated from England and Wales to another country outside the UK (up from 584,900 in the year to mid-2024)

*   net international migration to England and Wales was 211,700 (down from 612,500 in the year to mid-2024)

Our [Long-term international migration (LTIM), provisional: year ending December 2025 bulletin](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/internationalmigration/bulletins/longterminternationalmigrationprovisional/yearendingdecember2025) explains how, at the UK level, the main reason for the fall in net migration was because of fewer non-EU+ nationals arriving for work-related reasons.

We estimate that there were 5,900 net internal moves out of England and Wales to the rest of the UK in the year to mid-2025.

### Births and deaths

There was a decrease in the number of births and deaths in the year to mid-2025, compared with the previous year.

We estimate that:

*   there were 588,000 births, a decrease of 8,000 compared with mid-2024, and the fewest since mid-1978

*   there were 568,400 deaths, a decrease of 2,300 compared with mid-2024, and the fewest since mid-2019 before the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic

*   natural change, the difference between births and deaths, contributed an annual increase in the population of 19,600

These estimates differ slightly to other Office for National Statistics (ONS) birth and death statistics, which are reported by calendar year.

View recent population trends for local areas with our new interactive tool in Section 6: Local authorities.

Although estimated net international migration was lower in the year to mid-2025 compared with the previous year, it continued to contribute the most to population growth.

### Important information on using population estimates

Mid-year population estimates are produced using the cohort component method. This is a standard demographic method that estimates the size of the population using the components of population change to update a population base (in this case, using census estimates). A major strength of this method is that it is consistent over time and across geographical areas, and the components of population change are coherent with the resulting estimates.

However, a limitation of the methods used to produce population estimates is that they are subject to statistical uncertainty related to:

*   the measurement of the census base they are rolled forward from

*   the measurement of each component of population change

Statistical uncertainty is lowest immediately following a census, and greatest immediately before the next census. This is because errors accumulate over time as estimates are rolled forward onto the following year.

In general, the degree of uncertainty is higher for smaller geographies. More information can be found in our [Local authority quality of population estimates for England and Wales report](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/localauthorityqualityofpopulationestimatesforenglandandwales). Uncertainty is also greater for estimates with narrower bands of interest, such as estimates broken down by age and/or sex.

Data sources we use for the components of change are the best available at the time, that are also nationally consistent down to local authority level. Population estimates are produced using these components of change and are subject to the coverage and error associated with these sources.

Population estimates for mid-2022 onwards are subject to regular revision as the methods and data used to estimate international and internal migration continue to be developed. This means the figures in this bulletin might be different from previous and future releases.

Information on revisions can be found inSection 7: Revisions to population data.

Population estimates based on Census 2021 could also be affected by the impact of the coronavirus pandemic. More information can be found in our [Effect of the coronavirus pandemic on the quality of mid-year population estimates for England and Wales report](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/effectofthecoronaviruspandemiconthequalityofmidyearpopulationestimatesforenglandandwales).

More information on uncertainty can be found in our [Population estimates for England and Wales quality and methods guide](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesqualityandmethodsguide).

In our previous Population estimates for England and Wales: mid-2024 bulletin, we stated our intention for modelled admin-based population estimates (ABPEs) to become the official estimates of the population in 2026. This is no longer our aim. Instead, we will make iterative improvements to the data and methods that underpin the components of population change. These improvements will focus on internal migration and disaggregation of LTIM estimates to local authority level.

## 2. How to use these statistics

You can use these statistics:

*   for planning and monitoring service delivery, resource allocation, and managing the economy

*   as denominators for rates or ratios, for example, in health and economic indicators

With these statistics, you cannot:

*   add the most recent estimates to a time series from previous releases; the full time series associated with this release should be used

*   use them in conjunction with our mid-2025 provisional UK estimates, and estimates for Scotland, to find the mid-2025 population estimates for Northern Ireland

These estimates are subject to [statistical uncertainty](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesqualityandmethodsguide#quality-of-the-statistics), so small differences between areas or over time should be interpreted with caution, particularly for smaller geographies and detailed age-sex breakdowns.

These estimates will be revised in future releases as population estimates methods and data are improved, and once estimates from Census 2031 (England and Wales) are available. More information on improving estimates can be found in our [Improving population estimates for England and Wales article](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/improvingpopulationestimatesforenglandandwales).

1.   “Net-migration and other” includes international and internal migration, changes in armed forces personnel and dependants, and unattributable population change.

Since mid-1999, migration has contributed the most to population growth. Before this, population growth was mainly caused by natural change. At the country level, migration includes people moving to or from non-UK countries, people moving between UK countries, and changes in armed forces and dependants.

International migration is by far the largest component of migration. Lower levels of net migration in the year to mid-2020 are because of travel restrictions during the coronavirus pandemic. Net migration had remained relatively unchanged for three years before the pandemic period.

Overall, births have declined since mid-2012, except for brief increases in the years ending mid-2016 and mid-2022. Over the same period, deaths have generally increased, despite some annual decreases, including a 0.4% decrease in deaths in the latest year to mid-2025. The increasing number of deaths reflects the growing size of the population and the increasing number of older people.

## 4. Countries

The population of England was 58,834,800 in mid-2025, and the population of Wales was 3,175,200. There was population growth in England for the year to mid-2025. There was a small decrease in population in Wales, the first decrease since mid-2015. This resulted in:

*   an increase of 227,600 people (0.4%) in England
*   a decrease of 2,800 people (negative 0.1%) in Wales

For mid-2025, following three consecutive years of high population growth, the rate of population growth in England fell to a similar level to mid-2021.

### Contributors to population change

In England, net international migration was the main contributor to population growth in the year to mid-2025. Natural change (births minus deaths) also contributed to population growth, but to a lesser extent. Internal migration resulted in a net outflow of people from England to the rest of the UK.

For Wales, the largest contributor to the decrease in population was natural change (births minus deaths). International migration and internal migration both added to the population of Wales in mid-2025, but only partially offset the decrease in population from natural change.

### Age composition

The median (average) age in Wales is higher than in England. Over the last decade, the median age has increased by similar amounts in both countries, reaching 40.6 years in England, and 43.2 years in Wales, in mid-2025.

The age structure of the population is determined by the patterns of births, deaths and migration in previous years. The size of population cohorts at different ages varies.

#### Figure 5: Age structure of the UK population, mid-2011 to mid-2025

### Ageing population in England and Wales

The number of people aged 65 years and over in England increased by 216,200 (2.0%) in the year to mid-2025, accounting for 19.1% of the total population, compared with 16.4% in mid-2011.

The number of people aged 65 years and over in Wales increased by 10,800 (1.6%) in the year to mid-2025, accounting for 22.2% of the total population, compared with 18.5% of the population in mid-2011.

### Population aged 16 to 64 years

The number of people aged 16 to 64 years increased in England by 104,600 (0.3%), and decreased in Wales by 4,800 (0.2%), in the year to mid-2025.

This age group represented 63.0% of the population in England, and 61.0% of the population in Wales, in the year to mid-2025.

### Fewer children in the year to mid-2025

The number of people aged 15 years and under decreased in both countries, by 93,200 (0.9%) in England, and by 8,700 (1.6%) in Wales.

Children made up 17.9% of the population in England, and 16.5% of the population in Wales, in the year to mid-2025.

### Old-age-dependency ratio

Dependency ratios are used to inform government financial planning. The old-age-dependency ratio (OADR) is the number of people of pensionable age for every 1,000 people of working age.

In the year to mid-2025, the OADR was 283 for England and Wales overall. For England, the OADR was 280, and for Wales, it was 336.

### Estimates of the very old

Published alongside the mid-year estimates is our [Estimates of the very old, including centenarians, England and Wales: 2002 to 2025](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/estimatesoftheveryoldincludingcentenariansenglandandwales2002to2025). There were 15,172 centenarians (people aged 100 years and over) in England and Wales in 2025, an increase of 21.6% since 2015. There were 709 people aged 105 years and over in England and Wales in 2025, an increase of 34.0% since mid-2024. This growth is explained by the large generation born after World War One (born 1919 to 1920) reaching age 105 years.

### Population by sex

In England, there were an estimated 30.0 million females and 28.8 million males in the year to mid-2025, with the number of males increasing at a slightly faster rate than females since mid-2024 (0.4% and 0.3%, respectively). The changes in England were largely influenced by:

*   net international migration, which was 27,200 higher for males than for females
*   births, which were 14,600 higher for males than for females; it is normal to have roughly 105 male births for every 100 females, and this is the case for births in the year to mid-2025

In Wales, there were an estimated 1.62 million females and 1.55 million males, in the year to mid-2025. There was a small decrease in the total population of Wales by 2,800 compared with the previous year, an estimated decrease of 1,000 females and 1,800 males. The changes in Wales were largely influenced by:

*   net international migration, where there were more females than males migrating from other countries in the UK, but fewer females than males migrating from outside of the UK

*   deaths, which were 9,200 higher than births, with natural change (births minus deaths) being approximately the same for both males and females, at negative 4,600

!

We have revised population estimates for mid-2022, mid-2023 and mid-2024 to use updated data for international migration. Read more in Section 7: Revisions to population data.

## 5. Regions

All regions in England, except for London, had population growth in the year to mid-2025, with increases ranging between 0.28% and 0.74%. The North West had the highest rate of population growth, caused primarily by international migration and migration from other areas of the UK.

Although London had positive natural change (more births than deaths) and net international inward migration, this was more than offset by net outward migration to other areas of the UK. As a result, London's population decreased by 0.29% in the year to mid-2025, the first decrease since the year to mid-2021.

In the year to mid-2025, there were more births than deaths (positive natural change) in London, the West Midlands and the East of England. The other regions had negative natural change, which reflects a long-term decline in fertility and an increasing number of deaths because of the growing proportion of older people.

Revisions have been made to mid-2022, mid-2023, and mid-2024 population estimates to incorporate improved international migration data.

We have used the latest long-term international migration estimates, which were published in May 2026.

The total population estimates for England and Wales have been revised to:

*   61,155,900 in mid-2023, an increase of 56,000 (0.09%)

Estimates for males and females have changed:

*   the number of females is now 17,300 (0.06%) higher in mid-2022, 28,500 (0.09%) higher in mid-2023, and 3,900 (0.01%) lower in mid-2024

*   the number of males is now 26,500 (0.09%) higher in mid-2022, 27,500 (0.09%) higher in mid-2023, and 17,700 (0.06%) lower in mid-2024

By age group, the most notable revision changes are the decreases in those aged under 16 years:

*   40,800 (0.37%) lower for mid-2022, 89,700 (0.8%) lower for mid-2023, and 139,000 (1.23%) lower for mid-2024

By country, revised estimates for:

*   England are 45,300 (0.08%) higher for mid-2022, 58,300 (0.1%) higher for mid-2023, and 12,900 (0.02%) lower for mid-2024

*   Wales are 1,500 (0.05%) lower for mid-2022, 2,300 (0.07%) lower for mid-2023, and 8,600 (0.27%) lower for mid-2024

The impact of the revisions varies by local authority:

*   for mid-2023, the population in 27 local authorities was revised up by more than 0.5%, with none revised down by more than 0.5%

*   for mid-2024, the population in 27 local authorities was revised up by more than 0.5%, with 20 revised down by more than 0.5%

*   revised estimates almost exclusively fall within the uncertainty ranges of the unrevised estimates; the single exception is Boston for mid-2023, where the revised estimate is 152 higher than the upper interval of the unrevised estimate

## 8. Definitions

### Components of change

Components of change are the factors that contribute to population change. This includes births and deaths (commonly referred to as natural change) and net migration. Migration includes movements of people between England and Wales and the various countries of the world (international migration), and between local authority areas within the UK (internal migration).

### Internal migration

Describes moves made between local authorities, regions, or countries within the UK. Unlike international migration, there is no internationally agreed definition.

### International migration

We use the United Nations (UN) recommended definition of a long-term international migrant: "a person who moves to a country other than that of his or her usual residence for a period of at least a year (12 months), so that the country of destination effectively becomes his or her new country of usual residence."

Net international migration is the difference between the number of people moving into and out of England and Wales from outside the UK.

EU+ migration refers to the migration of people who hold EU nationality. Non-EU+ is the sum of the rest of the world, including the rest of Europe, not included in the EU+ category. British nationals are excluded from these numbers. More information is available in our [Long-term international migration, provisional: year ending December 2025 bulletin](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/internationalmigration/bulletins/longterminternationalmigrationprovisional/yearendingdecember2025#definitions).

### Median age

The age of the person in the middle of the group, such that one half of the group is younger than that person, and the other half is older.

### Mid-year population estimates

Population estimates produced using the cohort component method. This is a standard demographic method that estimates the size of the population using the components of population change to update a population base. These are [accredited official statistics](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/accredited-official-statistics/).

### Natural change

The difference between births and deaths. If natural change is greater than zero, then there have been more births than deaths. If natural change is negative, then there have been more deaths than births.

### Net migration

The difference between the number of people coming to live in an area (immigration), and the number of people leaving to live elsewhere (emigration). When more people are coming to the area than leaving, net migration is above zero and so adds to the population. Net migration takes account of both international and internal migration.

### Old-age-dependency ratio

The number of people of pensionable age (state pension age and over) for every 1,000 people of working age (aged 16 years and over but below state pension age).

### Rate of population change by component

We use these rates to compare how the different components of population change have contributed to changes in the size of the population in different areas. Rates for mid-2025 are calculated by dividing the estimated number of events for each component in the year to mid-2025 by the mid-2024 population estimate. We then multiply this figure by 100 to present the rate per 100 population.

The annual percentage change in the size of the population is the sum of all rates of change for each component. Figures may not sum exactly because of rounding.

### Usually resident population

These data estimate the "usually resident population". This is the standard United Nations definition as outlined in the [Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses (PDF, 3.76MB)](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/publication/SeriesM/Series_M67Rev4en.pdf). It includes only people who reside in a country for 12 months or more, making them usually resident in that country. Visitors and short-term migrants are excluded.

## 1. Overview

The population of England and Wales continued to grow in the year to mid-2025, reaching an estimated 62.0 million people. The size of the population is estimated to have increased by 224,900 (0.4%) from mid-2024, the lowest rate of increase since mid-2020. This was primarily because of a fall in international net migration, but natural change (births minus deaths) was also slightly lower in the year to mid-2025.

!

These estimates are subject to [statistical uncertainty](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesqualityandmethodsguide), particularly for smaller geographic areas and detailed age-sex breakdowns. We have published research-based measures of statistical uncertainty alongside the estimates, which can be found in our [accompanying datasets](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/populationestimatesforenglandandwales/mid2025/relateddata).

### Migration

The number of people immigrating to England and Wales from outside the UK decreased in the year to mid-2025, compared with the previous year. The number of people emigrating from England and Wales to outside the UK increased in the same period. This led to an overall decrease in net international migration compared with the previous year.

We estimate that in the year to mid-2025:

*   816,500 people immigrated to England and Wales from outside the UK (down from 1,197,500 in the year to mid-2024)

*   604,800 people emigrated from England and Wales to another country outside the UK (up from 584,900 in the year to mid-2024)

*   net international migration to England and Wales was 211,700 (down from 612,500 in the year to mid-2024)

Our [Long-term international migration (LTIM), provisional: year ending December 2025 bulletin](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/internationalmigration/bulletins/longterminternationalmigrationprovisional/yearendingdecember2025) explains how, at the UK level, the main reason for the fall in net migration was because of fewer non-EU+ nationals arriving for work-related reasons.

We estimate that there were 5,900 net internal moves out of England and Wales to the rest of the UK in the year to mid-2025.

### Births and deaths

There was a decrease in the number of births and deaths in the year to mid-2025, compared with the previous year.

We estimate that:

*   there were 588,000 births, a decrease of 8,000 compared with mid-2024, and the fewest since mid-1978

*   there were 568,400 deaths, a decrease of 2,300 compared with mid-2024, and the fewest since mid-2019 before the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic

*   natural change, the difference between births and deaths, contributed an annual increase in the population of 19,600

These estimates differ slightly to other Office for National Statistics (ONS) birth and death statistics, which are reported by calendar year.

View recent population trends for local areas with our new interactive tool in Section 6: Local authorities.

Although estimated net international migration was lower in the year to mid-2025 compared with the previous year, it continued to contribute the most to population growth.

### Important information on using population estimates

Mid-year population estimates are produced using the cohort component method. This is a standard demographic method that estimates the size of the population using the components of population change to update a population base (in this case, using census estimates). A major strength of this method is that it is consistent over time and across geographical areas, and the components of population change are coherent with the resulting estimates.

However, a limitation of the methods used to produce population estimates is that they are subject to statistical uncertainty related to:

*   the measurement of the census base they are rolled forward from

*   the measurement of each component of population change

Statistical uncertainty is lowest immediately following a census, and greatest immediately before the next census. This is because errors accumulate over time as estimates are rolled forward onto the following year.

In general, the degree of uncertainty is higher for smaller geographies. More information can be found in our [Local authority quality of population estimates for England and Wales report](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/localauthorityqualityofpopulationestimatesforenglandandwales). Uncertainty is also greater for estimates with narrower bands of interest, such as estimates broken down by age and/or sex.

Data sources we use for the components of change are the best available at the time, that are also nationally consistent down to local authority level. Population estimates are produced using these components of change and are subject to the coverage and error associated with these sources.

Population estimates for mid-2022 onwards are subject to regular revision as the methods and data used to estimate international and internal migration continue to be developed. This means the figures in this bulletin might be different from previous and future releases.

Information on revisions can be found inSection 7: Revisions to population data.

Population estimates based on Census 2021 could also be affected by the impact of the coronavirus pandemic. More information can be found in our [Effect of the coronavirus pandemic on the quality of mid-year population estimates for England and Wales report](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/effectofthecoronaviruspandemiconthequalityofmidyearpopulationestimatesforenglandandwales).

More information on uncertainty can be found in our [Population estimates for England and Wales quality and methods guide](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesqualityandmethodsguide).

In our previous Population estimates for England and Wales: mid-2024 bulletin, we stated our intention for modelled admin-based population estimates (ABPEs) to become the official estimates of the population in 2026. This is no longer our aim. Instead, we will make iterative improvements to the data and methods that underpin the components of population change. These improvements will focus on internal migration and disaggregation of LTIM estimates to local authority level.

## 2. How to use these statistics

You can use these statistics:

*   for planning and monitoring service delivery, resource allocation, and managing the economy

*   as denominators for rates or ratios, for example, in health and economic indicators

With these statistics, you cannot:

*   add the most recent estimates to a time series from previous releases; the full time series associated with this release should be used

*   use them in conjunction with our mid-2025 provisional UK estimates, and estimates for Scotland, to find the mid-2025 population estimates for Northern Ireland

These estimates are subject to [statistical uncertainty](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesqualityandmethodsguide#quality-of-the-statistics), so small differences between areas or over time should be interpreted with caution, particularly for smaller geographies and detailed age-sex breakdowns.

These estimates will be revised in future releases as population estimates methods and data are improved, and once estimates from Census 2031 (England and Wales) are available. More information on improving estimates can be found in our [Improving population estimates for England and Wales article](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/improvingpopulationestimatesforenglandandwales).

## 3. Comparisons over time

The population of England and Wales has increased each year since mid-1982. The greatest percentage increase over this period (1.4%) was in the year to mid-2023. The coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic led to smaller population increases in the years ending mid-2020 and mid-2021.

Since mid-1999, migration has contributed the most to population growth. Before this, population growth was mainly caused by natural change. At the country level, migration includes people moving to or from non-UK countries, people moving between UK countries, and changes in armed forces and dependants.

International migration is by far the largest component of migration. Lower levels of net migration in the year to mid-2020 are because of travel restrictions during the coronavirus pandemic. Net migration had remained relatively unchanged for three years before the pandemic period.

Overall, births have declined since mid-2012, except for brief increases in the years ending mid-2016 and mid-2022. Over the same period, deaths have generally increased, despite some annual decreases, including a 0.4% decrease in deaths in the latest year to mid-2025. The increasing number of deaths reflects the growing size of the population and the increasing number of older people.

## 4. Countries

The population of England was 58,834,800 in mid-2025, and the population of Wales was 3,175,200. There was population growth in England for the year to mid-2025. There was a small decrease in population in Wales, the first decrease since mid-2015. This resulted in:

*   an increase of 227,600 people (0.4%) in England
*   a decrease of 2,800 people (negative 0.1%) in Wales

For mid-2025, following three consecutive years of high population growth, the rate of population growth in England fell to a similar level to mid-2021.

### Contributors to population change

In England, net international migration was the main contributor to population growth in the year to mid-2025. Natural change (births minus deaths) also contributed to population growth, but to a lesser extent. Internal migration resulted in a net outflow of people from England to the rest of the UK.

For Wales, the largest contributor to the decrease in population was natural change (births minus deaths). International migration and internal migration both added to the population of Wales in mid-2025, but only partially offset the decrease in population from natural change.

### Age composition

The median (average) age in Wales is higher than in England. Over the last decade, the median age has increased by similar amounts in both countries, reaching 40.6 years in England, and 43.2 years in Wales, in mid-2025.

The age structure of the population is determined by the patterns of births, deaths and migration in previous years. The size of population cohorts at different ages varies.

### Ageing population in England and Wales

The number of people aged 65 years and over in England increased by 216,200 (2.0%) in the year to mid-2025, accounting for 19.1% of the total population, compared with 16.4% in mid-2011.

The number of people aged 65 years and over in Wales increased by 10,800 (1.6%) in the year to mid-2025, accounting for 22.2% of the total population, compared with 18.5% of the population in mid-2011.

### Population aged 16 to 64 years

The number of people aged 16 to 64 years increased in England by 104,600 (0.3%), and decreased in Wales by 4,800 (0.2%), in the year to mid-2025.

This age group represented 63.0% of the population in England, and 61.0% of the population in Wales, in the year to mid-2025.

### Fewer children in the year to mid-2025

The number of people aged 15 years and under decreased in both countries, by 93,200 (0.9%) in England, and by 8,700 (1.6%) in Wales.

Children made up 17.9% of the population in England, and 16.5% of the population in Wales, in the year to mid-2025.

### Old-age-dependency ratio

Dependency ratios are used to inform government financial planning. The old-age-dependency ratio (OADR) is the number of people of pensionable age for every 1,000 people of working age.

In the year to mid-2025, the OADR was 283 for England and Wales overall. For England, the OADR was 280, and for Wales, it was 336.

### Estimates of the very old

Published alongside the mid-year estimates is our [Estimates of the very old, including centenarians, England and Wales: 2002 to 2025](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/estimatesoftheveryoldincludingcentenariansenglandandwales2002to2025). There were 15,172 centenarians (people aged 100 years and over) in England and Wales in 2025, an increase of 21.6% since 2015. There were 709 people aged 105 years and over in England and Wales in 2025, an increase of 34.0% since mid-2024. This growth is explained by the large generation born after World War One (born 1919 to 1920) reaching age 105 years.

### Population by sex

In England, there were an estimated 30.0 million females and 28.8 million males in the year to mid-2025, with the number of males increasing at a slightly faster rate than females since mid-2024 (0.4% and 0.3%, respectively). The changes in England were largely influenced by:

*   net international migration, which was 27,200 higher for males than for females
*   births, which were 14,600 higher for males than for females; it is normal to have roughly 105 male births for every 100 females, and this is the case for births in the year to mid-2025

In Wales, there were an estimated 1.62 million females and 1.55 million males, in the year to mid-2025. There was a small decrease in the total population of Wales by 2,800 compared with the previous year, an estimated decrease of 1,000 females and 1,800 males. The changes in Wales were largely influenced by:

*   net international migration, where there were more females than males migrating from other countries in the UK, but fewer females than males migrating from outside of the UK

*   deaths, which were 9,200 higher than births, with natural change (births minus deaths) being approximately the same for both males and females, at negative 4,600

!

We have revised population estimates for mid-2022, mid-2023 and mid-2024 to use updated data for international migration. Read more in Section 7: Revisions to population data.

## 5. Regions

All regions in England, except for London, had population growth in the year to mid-2025, with increases ranging between 0.28% and 0.74%. The North West had the highest rate of population growth, caused primarily by international migration and migration from other areas of the UK.

Although London had positive natural change (more births than deaths) and net international inward migration, this was more than offset by net outward migration to other areas of the UK. As a result, London's population decreased by 0.29% in the year to mid-2025, the first decrease since the year to mid-2021.

In the year to mid-2025, there were more births than deaths (positive natural change) in London, the West Midlands and the East of England. The other regions had negative natural change, which reflects a long-term decline in fertility and an increasing number of deaths because of the growing proportion of older people.

## 7. Revisions to population data

### Revisions to population estimates for mid-2022, mid-2023 and mid-2024, England and Wales

Revisions have been made to mid-2022, mid-2023, and mid-2024 population estimates to incorporate improved international migration data.

We have used the latest long-term international migration estimates, which were published in May 2026.

The total population estimates for England and Wales have been revised to:

*   60,322,400 in mid-2022, an increase of 43,800 (0.07%)
*   61,155,900 in mid-2023, an increase of 56,000 (0.09%)
*   61,785,000 in mid-2024, a decrease of 21,600 (negative 0.03%)

These revisions fall within the [confidence intervals](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/measuresofstatisticaluncertaintysummary) for the pre-revised estimates.

Estimates for males and females have changed:

*   the number of females is now 17,300 (0.06%) higher in mid-2022, 28,500 (0.09%) higher in mid-2023, and 3,900 (0.01%) lower in mid-2024

*   the number of males is now 26,500 (0.09%) higher in mid-2022, 27,500 (0.09%) higher in mid-2023, and 17,700 (0.06%) lower in mid-2024

By age group, the most notable revision changes are the decreases in those aged under 16 years:

*   40,800 (0.37%) lower for mid-2022, 89,700 (0.8%) lower for mid-2023, and 139,000 (1.23%) lower for mid-2024

By country, revised estimates for:

*   England are 45,300 (0.08%) higher for mid-2022, 58,300 (0.1%) higher for mid-2023, and 12,900 (0.02%) lower for mid-2024

*   Wales are 1,500 (0.05%) lower for mid-2022, 2,300 (0.07%) lower for mid-2023, and 8,600 (0.27%) lower for mid-2024

### Local authority population estimates revisions

The impact of the revisions varies by local authority:

*   for mid-2022, the population in 20 local authorities was revised up by more than 0.5%, with none revised down by more than 0.5%

*   for mid-2023, the population in 27 local authorities was revised up by more than 0.5%, with none revised down by more than 0.5%

*   for mid-2024, the population in 27 local authorities was revised up by more than 0.5%, with 20 revised down by more than 0.5%

*   revised estimates almost exclusively fall within the uncertainty ranges of the unrevised estimates; the single exception is Boston for mid-2023, where the revised estimate is 152 higher than the upper interval of the unrevised estimate

Further information on the impact of revisions is available in our [accompanying datasets](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/populationestimatesforenglandandwales/mid2025/relateddata) and in our [Analysis of population estimates for UK tool](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/datasets/analysisofpopulationestimatestoolforuk). ## 8. Definitions

### Components of change

Components of change are the factors that contribute to population change. This includes births and deaths (commonly referred to as natural change) and net migration. Migration includes movements of people between England and Wales and the various countries of the world (international migration), and between local authority areas within the UK (internal migration).

### Internal migration

Describes moves made between local authorities, regions, or countries within the UK. Unlike international migration, there is no internationally agreed definition.

### International migration

We use the United Nations (UN) recommended definition of a long-term international migrant: "a person who moves to a country other than that of his or her usual residence for a period of at least a year (12 months), so that the country of destination effectively becomes his or her new country of usual residence."

Net international migration is the difference between the number of people moving into and out of England and Wales from outside the UK.

EU+ migration refers to the migration of people who hold EU nationality. Non-EU+ is the sum of the rest of the world, including the rest of Europe, not included in the EU+ category. British nationals are excluded from these numbers. More information is available in our [Long-term international migration, provisional: year ending December 2025 bulletin](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/internationalmigration/bulletins/longterminternationalmigrationprovisional/yearendingdecember2025#definitions).

### Median age

The age of the person in the middle of the group, such that one half of the group is younger than that person, and the other half is older.

### Mid-year population estimates

Population estimates produced using the cohort component method. This is a standard demographic method that estimates the size of the population using the components of population change to update a population base. These are [accredited official statistics](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/accredited-official-statistics/).

### Natural change

The difference between births and deaths. If natural change is greater than zero, then there have been more births than deaths. If natural change is negative, then there have been more deaths than births.

### Net migration

The difference between the number of people coming to live in an area (immigration), and the number of people leaving to live elsewhere (emigration). When more people are coming to the area than leaving, net migration is above zero and so adds to the population. Net migration takes account of both international and internal migration.

### Old-age-dependency ratio

The number of people of pensionable age (state pension age and over) for every 1,000 people of working age (aged 16 years and over but below state pension age).

### Rate of population change by component

We use these rates to compare how the different components of population change have contributed to changes in the size of the population in different areas. Rates for mid-2025 are calculated by dividing the estimated number of events for each component in the year to mid-2025 by the mid-2024 population estimate. We then multiply this figure by 100 to present the rate per 100 population.

The annual percentage change in the size of the population is the sum of all rates of change for each component. Figures may not sum exactly because of rounding.

### Usually resident population

These data estimate the "usually resident population". This is the standard United Nations definition as outlined in the [Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses (PDF, 3.76MB)](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/publication/SeriesM/Series_M67Rev4en.pdf). It includes only people who reside in a country for 12 months or more, making them usually resident in that country. Visitors and short-term migrants are excluded.

## The UK population at mid-year 2021 was estimated to be 67.0 million, an increase of 3.7 million (5.9%) on the population in mid-2011.

*   Over the 10 years between 2011 and 2021, the population of England increased by 6.5% to an estimated 56,536,000, the highest rate of the four countries of the UK; the estimated population of Northern Ireland increased by 5.0% to 1,905,000, Scotland by 3.4% to 5,480,000, and Wales by 1.4% to an estimated 3,105,000.
*   The mid-2021 population estimates for England, Wales and Northern Ireland are based on the 2021 censuses for England, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
*   For Scotland, the mid-2021 population estimates are rolled forward from mid-2020, as Scotland’s census was moved to 2022 because of the impact of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic; this means that population estimates based on Scotland’s Census 2022 are not yet available.

## 2.The UK population at mid-2021

We estimate the UK population in mid-2021 to be 67.0 million (67,026,292). This is an aggregate of the estimates for the four constituent countries. For England, Wales, and Northern Ireland these are the first mid-year population estimates based on the 2021 censuses for these countries. For Scotland the mid-2021 population estimates were rolled forward from mid-2020 as the census in Scotland took place in March 2022, a year later than the rest of the UK, because of the impact of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The mid-2021 population estimates are primarily based on the 2021 censuses (for England and Wales, and Northern Ireland). The usual resident population as at Census day (21 March 2021), by single year of age, is aged on to 30 June 2021 and then births, deaths and migration are accounted for.

Censuses provide the most accurate estimate of the population and therefore the reliability of mid-year estimates is very high immediately following a census. The figures will be revised in the next two years to include updated estimates for Scotland, incorporating the 2022 Census for Scotland. We will also incorporate revisions to international migration [data](https://finchannel.com/category/tech-2 "Technology") as we continue our transformation of population and migration statistics.

3.Population change for UK countries

All four countries of the UK saw population increases in the decade between mid-2011 and mid-2021. Table 1 shows the populations and summary statistics for each country of the UK. The highest percentage increase was in England where the population increased by 3.4 million, a rise of 6.5% between 2011 and 2021. Northern Ireland saw the next highest percentage increase of 5.0%, followed by Scotland at 3.4% and Wales at 1.4%.
Overall, England had the highest population density of the four countries of the UK at mid-2021. However, this includes a wide variation within England, where the population density in [London](https://britishreporter.com/ "British Reporter") was 5,596 people per square kilometre (km) and the South West was 240 people per square km.

The median age of the population in the UK was 40.7 years in mid-2021, a year higher than in mid-2011. The increase in median age over the decade was highest in Northern Ireland, though at 39.8 years, this was still the lowest of the countries in the UK. Wales had the highest median age at 43.1 years.

The population of the UK increased by approximately 11.1 million (19.8%) during the last fifty years and by approximately 3.7 million (5.9%) during the last decade. Population growth in the latest decade was lower than the previous decade in all four UK countries.

## 4.Population of England and Wales

The mid-2021 population estimate for England and Wales was 59,642,000, with the population for England at 56,536,000 and Wales at 3,105,000. Census 2021 for England and Wales took place on 21 March 2021 and the mid-year population estimates for England and Wales are based on these with adjustments made for ageing, births, deaths and migration in the 101 days until 30 June 2021.

During the period between census day and mid-year 2021, most restrictions related to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic were lifted. However, restrictions were lifted on different dates in England and Wales. Alongside the lifting of restrictions, COVID-19 vaccinations were made available to all adults. The rollout of vaccinations resulted in greater interaction between individuals and the administrative [data](https://finchannel.com/category/tech-2 "Technology") that we use to measure internal migration (movement between one part of the UK and another). We have adjusted our methods to account for this by using Census 2021 data. Full details on this can be found in our [Population estimates for the UK, mid-2021 methodology guide](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/populationestimatesfortheukmid2021methodsguide).

### Components of change between census day and mid-year 2021 in England and Wales

The mid-2021 estimates are based on Census 2021 and produced using the following method:

*   ageing on the estimates from Census 2021 for England and Wales, by single year of age and local authority
*   adding the births in England and Wales for the period between Census 2021 and mid-year 2021 (171,000) and subtracting deaths (132,000)
*   accounting for net international migration (1,000) and internal migration (5,000)
*   no adjustments for either prisoners or home or foreign armed forces personnel have been made

!

Estimates of international migration into and out of the UK are experimental and provisional. They are based on administrative and survey data using a range of data sources alongside an experimental methodology to provide estimates by age and sex at a local level. They contain a degree of uncertainty that we are unable to quantify at this time. We will revise estimates of international migration as our methods develop. The official Northern Ireland estimates of international migration, produced by NISRA, and included in the UK figures already have National Statistics status.

For the UK as a whole, net international migration for the year to mid-2021 was an estimated 173,000 and for England and Wales it was an estimated 156,000. However, net international migration for the quarter of the year between April and June 2021, for England and Wales, was close to zero (an estimate of around 1,000). This reflects seasonal patterns in migration and covers the period where international [travel](https://finchannel.com/category/travel-biz-news/ "Travel") was restricted following the coronavirus pandemic. [Home Office statistics on passenger arrivals into the UK](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/statistics-relating-to-passenger-arrivals-since-the-covid-19-outbreak-august-2022/statistics-relating-to-passenger-arrivals-in-the-united-kingdom-since-the-covid-19-outbreak-august-2022) show that air [travel](https://finchannel.com/category/travel-biz-news/ "Travel") began to recover from July 2021.

### Internal migration for England and Wales

In the period between Census day and mid-year 2021 we estimate that around 5,000 more people moved to England and Wales from the rest of the UK than left. This contrasts with most periods where a higher number of people move from England and Wales to other parts of the UK.

5.Upcoming population estimates

### Rebasing and reconciliation

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) will conduct [reconciliation work for mid-year population estimates](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/articles/rebasingandreconciliationofmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowingcensus2021englandandwales/2022) to understand how and why the estimates based on Census 2021 for England and Wales differ from those based on the mid-year estimates rolled forward from the 2011 Census. The insights gained will be used to improve the production of future population estimates and will result in a revised back series of population estimates for the period 2012 to 2020. This back series will increase the coherence between the census and mid-year estimates. The provisional publication date is early 2023 for reconciliation and spring 2023 for rebasing.

The Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency (NISRA) will conduct reconciliation and rebasing work to understand how and why the estimates based on Census 2021 for Northern Ireland differ from those based on the mid-year estimates rolled forward from the 2011 census. Further information can be found in [Mid-year population estimates for Northern Ireland: 2021](https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/2021-mid-year-population-estimates-northern-ireland).

### Mid-2022 population estimates

We plan to publish population estimates for England and Wales in Summer 2023. The Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency (NISRA) also plan to release mid-2022 population estimates in Summer 2023. Details of its release plans can be found in its [Population Statistics Work Plan](https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/population-statistics-work-plan-2022-23).

Mid-2022 population estimates for Scotland will be based primarily on the results of the 2022 Census adjusted for births, deaths and migration in the period between census day and mid-year and are currently scheduled to be published in winter 2023 to 2024.

## The UK population at mid-year 2021 was estimated to be 67.0 million, an increase of 3.7 million (5.9%) on the population in mid-2011.

*   Over the 10 years between 2011 and 2021, the population of England increased by 6.5% to an estimated 56,536,000, the highest rate of the four countries of the UK; the estimated population of Northern Ireland increased by 5.0% to 1,905,000, Scotland by 3.4% to 5,480,000, and Wales by 1.4% to an estimated 3,105,000.
*   The mid-2021 population estimates for England, Wales and Northern Ireland are based on the 2021 censuses for England, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
*   For Scotland, the mid-2021 population estimates are rolled forward from mid-2020, as Scotland’s census was moved to 2022 because of the impact of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic; this means that population estimates based on Scotland’s Census 2022 are not yet available.

## 2.The UK population at mid-2021

We estimate the UK population in mid-2021 to be 67.0 million (67,026,292). This is an aggregate of the estimates for the four constituent countries. For England, Wales, and Northern Ireland these are the first mid-year population estimates based on the 2021 censuses for these countries. For Scotland the mid-2021 population estimates were rolled forward from mid-2020 as the census in Scotland took place in March 2022, a year later than the rest of the UK, because of the impact of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The mid-2021 population estimates are primarily based on the 2021 censuses (for England and Wales, and Northern Ireland). The usual resident population as at Census day (21 March 2021), by single year of age, is aged on to 30 June 2021 and then births, deaths and migration are accounted for.

Censuses provide the most accurate estimate of the population and therefore the reliability of mid-year estimates is very high immediately following a census. The figures will be revised in the next two years to include updated estimates for Scotland, incorporating the 2022 Census for Scotland. We will also incorporate revisions to international migration [data](https://finchannel.com/category/tech-2 "Technology") as we continue our transformation of population and migration statistics.

3.Population change for UK countries

All four countries of the UK saw population increases in the decade between mid-2011 and mid-2021. Table 1 shows the populations and summary statistics for each country of the UK. The highest percentage increase was in England where the population increased by 3.4 million, a rise of 6.5% between 2011 and 2021. Northern Ireland saw the next highest percentage increase of 5.0%, followed by Scotland at 3.4% and Wales at 1.4%.
Overall, England had the highest population density of the four countries of the UK at mid-2021. However, this includes a wide variation within England, where the population density in [London](https://britishreporter.com/ "British Reporter") was 5,596 people per square kilometre (km) and the South West was 240 people per square km.

The median age of the population in the UK was 40.7 years in mid-2021, a year higher than in mid-2011. The increase in median age over the decade was highest in Northern Ireland, though at 39.8 years, this was still the lowest of the countries in the UK. Wales had the highest median age at 43.1 years.

Figure 1 shows the percentage change in population of the UK during the fifty-year period from mid-1971 to mid-2021. The population of the UK increased by approximately 11.1 million (19.8%) during the last fifty years and by approximately 3.7 million (5.9%) during the last decade. Population growth in the latest decade was lower than the previous decade in all four UK countries.

## 4.Population of England and Wales

The mid-2021 population estimate for England and Wales was 59,642,000, with the population for England at 56,536,000 and Wales at 3,105,000. Census 2021 for England and Wales took place on 21 March 2021 and the mid-year population estimates for England and Wales are based on these with adjustments made for ageing, births, deaths and migration in the 101 days until 30 June 2021.

During the period between census day and mid-year 2021, most restrictions related to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic were lifted. However, restrictions were lifted on different dates in England and Wales. Alongside the lifting of restrictions, COVID-19 vaccinations were made available to all adults. The rollout of vaccinations resulted in greater interaction between individuals and the administrative [data](https://finchannel.com/category/tech-2 "Technology") that we use to measure internal migration (movement between one part of the UK and another). We have adjusted our methods to account for this by using Census 2021 data. Full details on this can be found in our [Population estimates for the UK, mid-2021 methodology guide](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/populationestimatesfortheukmid2021methodsguide).

### Components of change between census day and mid-year 2021 in England and Wales

The mid-2021 estimates are based on Census 2021 and produced using the following method:

*   ageing on the estimates from Census 2021 for England and Wales, by single year of age and local authority
*   adding the births in England and Wales for the period between Census 2021 and mid-year 2021 (171,000) and subtracting deaths (132,000)
*   accounting for net international migration (1,000) and internal migration (5,000)
*   no adjustments for either prisoners or home or foreign armed forces personnel have been made

!

Estimates of international migration into and out of the UK are experimental and provisional. They are based on administrative and survey data using a range of data sources alongside an experimental methodology to provide estimates by age and sex at a local level. They contain a degree of uncertainty that we are unable to quantify at this time. We will revise estimates of international migration as our methods develop. The official Northern Ireland estimates of international migration, produced by NISRA, and included in the UK figures already have National Statistics status.

For the UK as a whole, net international migration for the year to mid-2021 was an estimated 173,000 and for England and Wales it was an estimated 156,000. However, net international migration for the quarter of the year between April and June 2021, for England and Wales, was close to zero (an estimate of around 1,000). This reflects seasonal patterns in migration and covers the period where international [travel](https://finchannel.com/category/travel-biz-news/ "Travel") was restricted following the coronavirus pandemic. [Home Office statistics on passenger arrivals into the UK](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/statistics-relating-to-passenger-arrivals-since-the-covid-19-outbreak-august-2022/statistics-relating-to-passenger-arrivals-in-the-united-kingdom-since-the-covid-19-outbreak-august-2022) show that air [travel](https://finchannel.com/category/travel-biz-news/ "Travel") began to recover from July 2021.

### Internal migration for England and Wales

In the period between Census day and mid-year 2021 we estimate that around 5,000 more people moved to England and Wales from the rest of the UK than left. This contrasts with most periods where a higher number of people move from England and Wales to other parts of the UK.

5.Upcoming population estimates

### Rebasing and reconciliation

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) will conduct [reconciliation work for mid-year population estimates](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/articles/rebasingandreconciliationofmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowingcensus2021englandandwales/2022) to understand how and why the estimates based on Census 2021 for England and Wales differ from those based on the mid-year estimates rolled forward from the 2011 Census. The insights gained will be used to improve the production of future population estimates and will result in a revised back series of population estimates for the period 2012 to 2020. This back series will increase the coherence between the census and mid-year estimates. The provisional publication date is early 2023 for reconciliation and spring 2023 for rebasing.

The Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency (NISRA) will conduct reconciliation and rebasing work to understand how and why the estimates based on Census 2021 for Northern Ireland differ from those based on the mid-year estimates rolled forward from the 2011 census. Further information can be found in [Mid-year population estimates for Northern Ireland: 2021](https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/2021-mid-year-population-estimates-northern-ireland).

### Mid-2022 population estimates

We plan to publish population estimates for England and Wales in Summer 2023. The Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency (NISRA) also plan to release mid-2022 population estimates in Summer 2023. Details of its release plans can be found in its [Population Statistics Work Plan](https://www.nisra.gov.uk/publications/population-statistics-work-plan-2022-23).

Mid-2022 population estimates for Scotland will be based primarily on the results of the 2022 Census adjusted for births, deaths and migration in the period between census day and mid-year and are currently scheduled to be published in winter 2023 to 2024.

# Mid-year population estimates for England and Wales

**Published:** 11 May 2026

*   [Compliance review](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/publications/?publication_type=compliance-review)

## Findings

### ONS’s decision to continue with its current methods

On 4 March, ONS announced that it no longer plans to move to the ABPEs in summer 2026 and will instead focus on continuous improvement activity for the MYEs. ONS’s transparent communication of the decision, using the criteria[recommended by OSR](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/publication/admin-based-population-estimates-for-england-and-wales/pages/3/), demonstrated a clear commitment to support user understanding and confidence in its decision-making processes.

The decision to continue with the MYEs as the official headline population estimates is a significant pivot away from ONS’s previous ambition to make the ABPEs the official headline measure. As outlined[in our response letter](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/correspondence/ed-humpherson-to-mary-gregory-response-to-ons-plans-for-mid-year-population-estimates/), the announcement highlighted important areas for improvement within the current system, such as for the methods used to estimate internal migration and disaggregate long-term international migration at a local authority level.

These known limitations with the current methods (described in more detail in the section on[user confidence in subnational and sub-population](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/publication/mid-year-population-estimates-for-england-and-wales/pages/4/#_User_confidence_in)) may lead some users to question the continued reliance on existing methods. It is therefore important that ONS clarifies the strengths and limitations of the methods and develops new strategic goals and objectives to help drive the work forward.

Requirement 1: To support user confidence in its decision to continue with the MYEs, ONS must be open and explicit about the strengths and limitations of the current methods and what action ONS is taking, with time scales, to address methodological limitations with independent assurance.

ONS is currently hosting internal workshops to develop revised research plans for alternative approaches to population estimates, drawing on the insight gleaned from the development of the ABPEs and planned improvements to internal migration and the disaggregation of international migration. Publishing these revised plans, which are clearly aligned to ONS’s goals and objectives, will help ensure users remain well informed in an open and transparent way.
