For mid-2025, following three consecutive years of high population growth, the rate of population growth in England fell to a similar level to mid-2021.

### Contributors to population change

In England, net international migration was the main contributor to population growth in the year to mid-2025. Natural change (births minus deaths) also contributed to population growth, but to a lesser extent. Internal migration resulted in a net outflow of people from England to the rest of the UK.

For Wales, the largest contributor to the decrease in population was natural change (births minus deaths). International migration and internal migration both added to the population of Wales in mid-2025, but only partially offset the decrease in population from natural change.

### Age composition

The median (average) age in Wales is higher than in England. Over the last decade, the median age has increased by similar amounts in both countries, reaching 40.6 years in England, and 43.2 years in Wales, in mid-2025.

The age structure of the population is determined by the patterns of births, deaths and migration in previous years. The size of population cohorts at different ages varies.

### Ageing population in England and Wales

The number of people aged 65 years and over in England increased by 216,200 (2.0%) in the year to mid-2025, accounting for 19.1% of the total population, compared with 16.4% in mid-2011.

The number of people aged 65 years and over in Wales increased by 10,800 (1.6%) in the year to mid-2025, accounting for 22.2% of the total population, compared with 18.5% of the population in mid-2011.

### Population aged 16 to 64 years

The number of people aged 16 to 64 years increased in England by 104,600 (0.3%), and decreased in Wales by 4,800 (0.2%), in the year to mid-2025.

This age group represented 63.0% of the population in England, and 61.0% of the population in Wales, in the year to mid-2025.

### Fewer children in the year to mid-2025

The number of people aged 15 years and under decreased in both countries, by 93,200 (0.9%) in England, and by 8,700 (1.6%) in Wales.

Children made up 17.9% of the population in England, and 16.5% of the population in Wales, in the year to mid-2025.

### Old-age-dependency ratio

Dependency ratios are used to inform government financial planning. The old-age-dependency ratio (OADR) is the number of people of pensionable age for every 1,000 people of working age.

In the year to mid-2025, the OADR was 283 for England and Wales overall. For England, the OADR was 280, and for Wales, it was 336.

### Estimates of the very old

Published alongside the mid-year estimates is our [Estimates of the very old, including centenarians, England and Wales: 2002 to 2025](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/estimatesoftheveryoldincludingcentenariansenglandandwales2002to2025). There were 15,172 centenarians (people aged 100 years and over) in England and Wales in 2025, an increase of 21.6% since 2015. There were 709 people aged 105 years and over in England and Wales in 2025, an increase of 34.0% since mid-2024. This growth is explained by the large generation born after World War One (born 1919 to 1920) reaching age 105 years.

### Population by sex

In England, there were an estimated 30.0 million females and 28.8 million males in the year to mid-2025, with the number of males increasing at a slightly faster rate than females since mid-2024 (0.4% and 0.3%, respectively). The changes in England were largely influenced by:

*   net international migration, which was 27,200 higher for males than for females
*   births, which were 14,600 higher for males than for females; it is normal to have roughly 105 male births for every 100 females, and this is the case for births in the year to mid-2025

In Wales, there were an estimated 1.62 million females and 1.55 million males, in the year to mid-2025. There was a small decrease in the total population of Wales by 2,800 compared with the previous year, an estimated decrease of 1,000 females and 1,800 males. The changes in Wales were largely influenced by:

*   net international migration, where there were more females than males migrating from other countries in the UK, but fewer females than males migrating from outside of the UK

*   deaths, which were 9,200 higher than births, with natural change (births minus deaths) being approximately the same for both males and females, at negative 4,600

!

We have revised population estimates for mid-2022, mid-2023 and mid-2024 to use updated data for international migration. Read more in Section 7: Revisions to population data.

## 5. Regions

All regions in England, except for London, had population growth in the year to mid-2025, with increases ranging between 0.28% and 0.74%. The North West had the highest rate of population growth, caused primarily by international migration and migration from other areas of the UK.

Although London had positive natural change (more births than deaths) and net international inward migration, this was more than offset by net outward migration to other areas of the UK. As a result, London's population decreased by 0.29% in the year to mid-2025, the first decrease since the year to mid-2021.

In the year to mid-2025, there were more births than deaths (positive natural change) in London, the West Midlands and the East of England. The other regions had negative natural change, which reflects a long-term decline in fertility and an increasing number of deaths because of the growing proportion of older people.

## 7. Revisions to population data

### Revisions to population estimates for mid-2022, mid-2023 and mid-2024, England and Wales

Revisions have been made to mid-2022, mid-2023, and mid-2024 population estimates to incorporate improved international migration data.

We have used the latest long-term international migration estimates, which were published in May 2026.

The total population estimates for England and Wales have been revised to:

*   60,322,400 in mid-2022, an increase of 43,800 (0.07%)
*   61,155,900 in mid-2023, an increase of 56,000 (0.09%)
*   61,785,000 in mid-2024, a decrease of 21,600 (negative 0.03%)

These revisions fall within the [confidence intervals](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/measuresofstatisticaluncertaintysummary) for the pre-revised estimates.

Estimates for males and females have changed:

*   the number of females is now 17,300 (0.06%) higher in mid-2022, 28,500 (0.09%) higher in mid-2023, and 3,900 (0.01%) lower in mid-2024

*   the number of males is now 26,500 (0.09%) higher in mid-2022, 27,500 (0.09%) higher in mid-2023, and 17,700 (0.06%) lower in mid-2024

By age group, the most notable revision changes are the decreases in those aged under 16 years:

*   40,800 (0.37%) lower for mid-2022, 89,700 (0.8%) lower for mid-2023, and 139,000 (1.23%) lower for mid-2024

By country, revised estimates for:

*   England are 45,300 (0.08%) higher for mid-2022, 58,300 (0.1%) higher for mid-2023, and 12,900 (0.02%) lower for mid-2024

*   Wales are 1,500 (0.05%) lower for mid-2022, 2,300 (0.07%) lower for mid-2023, and 8,600 (0.27%) lower for mid-2024

### Local authority population estimates revisions

The impact of the revisions varies by local authority:

*   for mid-2022, the population in 20 local authorities was revised up by more than 0.5%, with none revised down by more than 0.5%

*   for mid-2023, the population in 27 local authorities was revised up by more than 0.5%, with none revised down by more than 0.5%

*   for mid-2024, the population in 27 local authorities was revised up by more than 0.5%, with 20 revised down by more than 0.5%

*   revised estimates almost exclusively fall within the uncertainty ranges of the unrevised estimates; the single exception is Boston for mid-2023, where the revised estimate is 152 higher than the upper interval of the unrevised estimate

Further information on the impact of revisions is available in our [accompanying datasets](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/populationestimatesforenglandandwales/mid2025/relateddata) and in our [Analysis of population estimates for UK tool](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/datasets/analysisofpopulationestimatestoolforuk). Using our analysis tool, you can explore the full impact of revisions for each area broken down by internal and international migration flows, single year of age, and sex.

## 8. Definitions

### Components of change

Components of change are the factors that contribute to population change. This includes births and deaths (commonly referred to as natural change) and net migration. Migration includes movements of people between England and Wales and the various countries of the world (international migration), and between local authority areas within the UK (internal migration).

### Internal migration

Describes moves made between local authorities, regions, or countries within the UK. Unlike international migration, there is no internationally agreed definition.

### International migration

We use the United Nations (UN) recommended definition of a long-term international migrant: "a person who moves to a country other than that of his or her usual residence for a period of at least a year (12 months), so that the country of destination effectively becomes his or her new country of usual residence."

Net international migration is the difference between the number of people moving into and out of England and Wales from outside the UK.

EU+ migration refers to the migration of people who hold EU nationality. Non-EU+ is the sum of the rest of the world, including the rest of Europe, not included in the EU+ category. British nationals are excluded from these numbers. More information is available in our [Long-term international migration, provisional: year ending December 2025 bulletin](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/internationalmigration/bulletins/longterminternationalmigrationprovisional/yearendingdecember2025#definitions).

### Median age

The age of the person in the middle of the group, such that one half of the group is younger than that person, and the other half is older.

### Mid-year population estimates

Population estimates produced using the cohort component method. This is a standard demographic method that estimates the size of the population using the components of population change to update a population base. These are [accredited official statistics](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/accredited-official-statistics/).

### Natural change

The difference between births and deaths. If natural change is greater than zero, then there have been more births than deaths. If natural change is negative, then there have been more deaths than births.

### Net migration

The difference between the number of people coming to live in an area (immigration), and the number of people leaving to live elsewhere (emigration). When more people are coming to the area than leaving, net migration is above zero and so adds to the population. Net migration takes account of both international and internal migration.

### Old-age-dependency ratio

The number of people of pensionable age (state pension age and over) for every 1,000 people of working age (aged 16 years and over but below state pension age).

### Rate of population change by component

We use these rates to compare how the different components of population change have contributed to changes in the size of the population in different areas. Rates for mid-2025 are calculated by dividing the estimated number of events for each component in the year to mid-2025 by the mid-2024 population estimate. We then multiply this figure by 100 to present the rate per 100 population.

The annual percentage change in the size of the population is the sum of all rates of change for each component. Figures may not sum exactly because of rounding.

### Usually resident population

These data estimate the "usually resident population". This is the standard United Nations definition as outlined in the [Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses (PDF, 3.76MB)](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/publication/SeriesM/Series_M67Rev4en.pdf). It includes only people who reside in a country for 12 months or more, making them usually resident in that country. Visitors and short-term migrants are excluded.

# Mid year estimates of the population: 2025

Mid-year population estimates for Wales by local authority, age and components of population change.

**First published:** 29 July 2026 

**Last updated:**29 July 2026

Print this page

## In this page

*   Introduction
*   Main points
*   Components of population change
*   Population by age
*   Population by local authority
*   Admin-based population estimates
*   Population estimates for the UK
*   Quality and methodology information
*   Contact details

## Introduction

[The Office for National Statistics (ONS) has published mid-2025 population estimates for Wales and England](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesmid2025). This bulletin refers specifically to estimates for Wales.

All data in this report are from mid-year estimates taken on 30 June of the relevant year. When we refer to estimates for 2025, for example, this means mid-2025 estimates, or estimates as at 30 June 2025. Data in this release mainly refer to 30 June 2025, with comparisons to the previous year (30 June 2024).

Estimates for 2022 to 2024 have been revised by the ONS to incorporate improved international migration data.

More information about the impact of the revisions are in the [ONS bulletin 'Population estimates for England and Wales: mid-2025'](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesmid2025).

The population estimates for Wales have been revised downwards to:

*   3,132,700 in 2022, a decrease of 1,500 (0.05%) from the previously published estimate
*   3,165,100 in 2023, a decrease of 2,300 (0.07%) from the previously published estimate
*   3,177,900 in 2024, a decrease of 8,600 (0.27%) from the previously published estimate

## Main points

*   Around 3,175,200 people were living in Wales, a small decrease of 0.1%, around 2,800 fewer people; this is the first decrease in population since between 2014 and 2015.
*   The recent population decrease has been driven by negative natural change and decreasing net international migration.
*   Over a fifth of people were aged 65 or older (22.2%, or 705,100 people).
*   Newport saw the largest percentage population increase (up 0.7%).
*   There was a population increase of 0.4% in England for the same period.

### Figure 1: population estimates for Wales, 1995 to 2025 [Note 1] [Note 2]

Image

![Image 2](https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/2026-07/figure-1-population-estimates-for-wales-1995-to-2025.svg)

Description of figure 1: this line chart shows that, since 1995, the population of Wales is estimated to have increased from 2.89 million to 3.18 million by 2025. Since 2021, the population has risen more sharply before decreasing in the latest year.

Source: Population estimates from the ONS.

[Note 1] The figures for 2022 to 2024 have been revised.

[Note 2] The y axis on this chart does not start at zero.

## Components of population change

Components of population change are the factors that contribute to population change. This includes births and deaths, commonly referred to as natural change, and net migration.

### Net migration

Net migration is the difference between the number of people coming to live in an area (immigration) and the number of people leaving to live elsewhere (emigration).

When more people are coming into the area than leaving, net migration is above zero and so adds to the population.

Net migration takes account of both international and internal migration.

### Internal migration

Internal migration is movements between local authorities in the UK.

### International migration

International migration is movements between Wales and the other countries of the world outside the UK.

### Figure 2: net internal and international migration estimates for Wales, 2005 to 2025 [Note 1]

Image

![Image 3](https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/2026-07/figure-2-net-internal-and-international-migration-estimates-for-wales-2005-to-2025.svg)

Description of figure 2: this line chart shows that net international migration has decreased by nearly 90% in 2025 compared with the previous year. Net internal migration increased slightly in 2025 compared with the previous year. Since 2020, migration patterns have changed. Net internal migration peaked during the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, while net international migration has been greater than net internal migration in the years since 2021 to 2024. In the latest year, net international migration was lower than net internal migration.

Source: Population estimates from the ONS.

[Note 1] The figures for 2022 to 2024 have been revised.

Net international migration to Wales was around 1,700 between 2024 and 2025. This is a decrease of nearly 90% compared with the previous year. It is at its lowest level since 2010.

The '[long-term international migration, provisional: year ending December 2025' release from the ONS](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/internationalmigration/bulletins/longterminternationalmigrationprovisional/yearendingdecember2025) explains how, at the UK level, net migration has declined. This is because fewer non-EU+ nationals arrived on work-related visas.

Net internal migration to Wales from the other UK nations, was around 4,900 between 2024 and 2025. This is a slight increase (up by 1.6%) from the previous year (4,800).

### Figure 3: births and deaths in Wales, 2005 to 2025 [Note 1]

Image

![Image 4](https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/2026-07/figure-3-births-and-deaths-in-wales-2005-to-2025.svg)

Description of figure 3: this line chart shows that, between 2006 and 2017, the number of births was higher than the number of deaths. Since that period, the number of deaths has outnumbered the number of births. Since 2011, the number of births has steadily decreased. The number of deaths has been increasing generally during the same period.

Source: Population estimates from the ONS.

[Note 1] The y axis on this chart does not start at zero.

Between 2024 and 2025, there continued to be more deaths than births, or negative natural change. There were around 35,600 deaths between 2024 and 2025.

The number of births between 2024 and 2025 was around 26,500, a decrease of around 1,000 compared with the previous year.

## Population by age

### Figure 4: population broad age group, 2005 to 2025 [Note 1]

Image

![Image 5](https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/2026-07/figure-4-population-broad-age-group-2005-to-2025.svg)

Description of figure 4: this stacked bar chart shows that, since 2005, the percentage of the population aged 65 years or older has increased, while the percentage of children and young people aged 0 to 15 years old has decreased slightly. The percentage of people aged 16 to 64 years old has also decreased slightly during the same period.

Source: Population estimates from the ONS.

[Note 1] The figures for 2022 to 2024 have been revised.

Over a fifth of people were aged 65 or older (22.2%, or 705,100 people) in 2025. Since 2015, the number of people aged 65 or older has increased by 13.6%. The number of people aged 75 years or older has increased by over a quarter during the same period, up 26.0%. This increased from around 276,400 people in 2015 to around 348,300 people in 2025.

61.0% of the population were aged 16 to 64 years old in 2025, around 1,936,200 people. This number has increased by 1.9% since 2015.

The remaining 16.8% of the population were children and young people aged 0 to 15 (around 533,900). This has decreased by 3.2% since 2015.

## Population by local authority

These estimates are subject to statistical uncertainty, particularly for smaller geographic areas and detailed age-sex breakdowns. The ONS has published research-based measures of statistical uncertainty alongside the estimates, which can be found in the accompanying datasets.

You can use the interactive tool on the ONS website to view the latest population estimates, and measures of statistical uncertainty, for your local area.The population decreased in all but 7 of the 22 local authorities between 2024 and 2025. The largest increases were in:

*   Newport (0.7% increase)
*   Denbighshire (0.4% increase)
*   Monmouthshire (0.2% increase)

The largest decreases were in:

*   Merthyr Tydfil (0.6% decrease)
*   Swansea (0.5% decrease)
*   Neath Port Talbot (0.4% decrease)

Cardiff and Newport were the only local authorities who saw more births than deaths between 2024 and 2025.

7 out of the 22 local authorities saw positive net international migration between 2024 and 2025. 16 out of 22 local authorities saw positive net internal migration.

### Figure 5: percentage population change in Wales between 2024 and 2025, by local authority

Image

![Image 6](https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/2026-07/figure-5-percentage-population-change-in-wales-between-2024-and-2025-by-local-authority_0.svg)

Description of figure 5: this map shows that Newport and Denbighshire have seen the largest percentage increase in their population between 2024 and 2025.

Source: Population estimates from the ONS.

## Admin-based population estimates

[On 4 March, the ONS published its quarterly update on population and migration statistics](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/articles/quarterlyupdateonpopulationandmigrationstatistics/march2026). Within this article, it said that admin-based population estimates were not being adopted as official estimates of the population.

It concluded that established methods for the mid-year population estimates should continue to be used, following a review against the published decision criteria and the announcement of a census in 2031. These methods are outlined in the [population estimates for England and Wales, mid-2025: methods guide (ONS)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesmid2022methodsguide). Using the established methods will ensure that population estimates can be produced reliably, with efficient and sustainable systems and processes.

The ONS will be moving to a model of continuous improvement of the population estimates, drawing on the research and experiences of developing ABPEs. They will make iterative improvements to the data and methods that underpin the components of population change, with a focus on internal migration and disaggregation of long-term international migration estimates to local authority level. More information can be found in the [quarterly update on population and migration statistics (ONS)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/articles/quarterlyupdateonpopulationandmigrationstatistics/march2026).

### UK population estimates, mid-2025

The ONS aims to publish a [full set of UK population estimates (ONS)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/annualmidyearpopulationestimates/previousreleases) for 2025 in autumn 2026. Northern Ireland’s population estimates for 2025 are due to be published in September to October.

## Quality and methodology information

### Mid-year population estimates

Population estimates are produced using the cohort component method. This is a standard demographic method that estimates the size of the population using the components of population change, like the census estimate, to update a population base. These are [accredited official statistics (Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR))](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/accredited-official-statistics/).

A limitation of the cohort component method used to produce population estimates is that they are subject to statistical uncertainty related to:

*   the measurement of the census base they are rolled forward from
*   the measurement of each component of population change

Statistical uncertainty is lowest immediately following a census, and greatest immediately before the next census. This is because errors accumulate over time as estimates are rolled forward onto the following year. To find out more see [population estimates for England and Wales quality and methods guide (ONS)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesqualityandmethodsguide).

### Usually resident population

These data estimate the ‘usually resident population’. This is the standard United Nations definition outlined on page 40 in the [Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses (UN)](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/demographic-social/Standards-and-Methods/files/Principles_and_Recommendations/Population-and-Housing-Censuses/Series_M67rev3-E.pdf#page=56). It only includes people who reside in a country for 12 months or more, making them usually resident in that country. Visitors and short-term migrants are excluded.

### Official statistics status

All official statistics should show the standards of the [Code of Practice for Statistics (UK Statistics Authority)](https://code.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/).

The mid-year estimates of the population are accredited official statistics, published by the ONS. They comply with the standards of trustworthiness, quality and value in the Code of Practice for Statistics. [On 11 May 2026, the OSR published a compliance check of mid-year population estimates for England and Wales](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/publication/mid-year-population-estimates-for-england-and-wales/).

It is the Welsh Government’s responsibility to maintain compliance with the standards expected of accreditation. If we become concerned about whether these statistics are still meeting the appropriate standards, we will discuss any concerns with OSR promptly. Accreditation can be cancelled or suspended at any point when the highest standards are not maintained, and reinstated when standards are restored.

Accredited official statistics are called National Statistics in the Statistics and Registration Service Act 2007.

### Statement of compliance with the Code of Practice for Statistics

Our statistical practice is regulated by the OSR. OSR sets the standards of trustworthiness, quality and value in the Code of Practice for Statistics that all producers of official statistics should adhere to.

All of our statistics are produced and published in accordance with a number of statements and protocols to enhance trustworthiness, quality and value. These are set out in the Welsh Government’s [Statement of Compliance](https://www.gov.wales/about-statistics-and-research#Statementofcompliance).

These [accredited official statistics (OSR)](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/policies/official-statistics-policies/accredited-official-statistics-policy/) demonstrate the standards expected around trustworthiness, quality and public value in the following ways.

#### Quality

Mid-year estimates of the population are produced by the Office for National statistics. Quality assurance of the population estimates for Wales is performed by Welsh Government statisticians. The statistical bulletin is then drafted, signed off by senior statisticians and published in line with the statement on confidentiality and data access which is informed by the trustworthiness pillar contained in the [Code of Practice for Statistics (UK Statistics Authority)](https://code.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/).

For further information about how these accredited official statistics, published by the ONS, demonstrate the standards expected around trustworthiness, quality and public value, see the [Population estimates for England and Wales quality and methods guide (ONS)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesqualityandmethodsguide).

You are welcome to contact us directly with any comments about how we meet these standards. Alternatively, you can contact OSR by emailing [regulation@statistics.gov.uk](mailto:regulation@statistics.gov.uk) or via the [OSR website](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/).

### Well-being of Future Generations Act (WFG)

The Well-being of Future Generations Act 2015 is about improving the social, economic, environmental, and cultural wellbeing of Wales. The Act puts in place seven wellbeing goals for Wales. These are for a more equal, prosperous, resilient, healthier, and globally responsible Wales, with cohesive communities and a vibrant culture and thriving Welsh language. Under section (10)(1) of the Act, the Welsh Ministers must (a) publish indicators (“national indicators”) that must be applied for the purpose of measuring progress towards the achievement of the wellbeing goals, and (b) lay a copy of the national indicators before Senedd Cymru. Under section 10(8) of the Well-being of Future Generations Act, where the Welsh Ministers revise the national indicators, they must as soon as reasonably practicable (a) publish the indicators as revised and (b) lay a copy of them before the Senedd. These national indicators were laid before the Senedd in 2021. The indicators laid on 14 December 2021 replace the set laid on 16 March 2016.

Information on the indicators, along with narratives for each of the wellbeing goals and associated technical information is available in the [Wellbeing of Wales report](https://www.gov.wales/wellbeing-wales).

As a national indicator under the Act, they must be referred to in the analyses of local wellbeing produced by public services boards when they are analysing the state of economic, social, environmental, and cultural wellbeing in their areas.

The Act states national milestones must be set that “…the Welsh Ministers consider would assist in measuring whether progress is being made towards the achievement of the wellbeing goals.” In doing so Welsh Ministers must specify how we know that a national milestone has been achieved and the time by which it is to be achieved.

National milestones are not performance targets for any individual organisation but are collective measures of success for Wales.

Some of the national indicators and national milestones use the mid-year estimates of the population as denominators, to calculate rates, for example.

Further information on the [Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015](https://www.gov.wales/well-being-future-generations-wales-act-2015-guidance).

The statistics included in this release could also provide supporting narrative to the national indicators and be used by public services boards in relation to their local wellbeing assessments and local wellbeing plans.

## Introduction

[The Office for National Statistics (ONS) has published mid-2025 population estimates for Wales and England](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesmid2025). This bulletin refers specifically to estimates for Wales.

All data in this report are from mid-year estimates taken on 30 June of the relevant year. When we refer to estimates for 2025, for example, this means mid-2025 estimates, or estimates as at 30 June 2025. Data in this release mainly refer to 30 June 2025, with comparisons to the previous year (30 June 2024).

Estimates for 2022 to 2024 have been revised by the ONS to incorporate improved international migration data.

More information about the impact of the revisions are in the [ONS bulletin 'Population estimates for England and Wales: mid-2025'](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesmid2025).

The population estimates for Wales have been revised downwards to:

*   3,132,700 in 2022, a decrease of 1,500 (0.05%) from the previously published estimate
*   3,165,100 in 2023, a decrease of 2,300 (0.07%) from the previously published estimate
*   3,177,900 in 2024, a decrease of 8,600 (0.27%) from the previously published estimate

## Main points

*   Around 3,175,200 people were living in Wales, a small decrease of 0.1%, around 2,800 fewer people; this is the first decrease in population since between 2014 and 2015.
*   The recent population decrease has been driven by negative natural change and decreasing net international migration.
*   Over a fifth of people were aged 65 or older (22.2%, or 705,100 people).
*   Newport saw the largest percentage population increase (up 0.7%).
*   There was a population increase of 0.4% in England for the same period.

## Components of population change

Components of population change are the factors that contribute to population change. This includes births and deaths, commonly referred to as natural change, and net migration.

### Net migration

Net migration is the difference between the number of people coming to live in an area (immigration) and the number of people leaving to live elsewhere (emigration).

When more people are coming into the area than leaving, net migration is above zero and so adds to the population.

Net migration takes account of both international and internal migration.

### Internal migration

Internal migration is movements between local authorities in the UK.

### International migration

International migration is movements between Wales and the other countries of the world outside the UK.

### Figure 2: net internal and international migration estimates for Wales, 2005 to 2025 [Note 1]

Image

![Image 3](https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/2026-07/figure-2-net-internal-and-international-migration-estimates-for-wales-2005-to-2025.svg)

Description of figure 2: this line chart shows that net international migration has decreased by nearly 90% in 2025 compared with the previous year. Net internal migration increased slightly in 2025 compared with the previous year. Since 2020, migration patterns have changed. Net internal migration peaked during the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, while net international migration has been greater than net internal migration in the years since 2021 to 2024. In the latest year, net international migration was lower than net internal migration.

Source: Population estimates from the ONS.

[Note 1] The figures for 2022 to 2024 have been revised.

Net international migration to Wales was around 1,700 between 2024 and 2025. This is a decrease of nearly 90% compared with the previous year. It is at its lowest level since 2010.

The '[long-term international migration, provisional: year ending December 2025' release from the ONS](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/internationalmigration/bulletins/longterminternationalmigrationprovisional/yearendingdecember2025) explains how, at the UK level, net migration has declined. This is because fewer non-EU+ nationals arrived on work-related visas.

Net internal migration to Wales from the other UK nations, was around 4,900 between 2024 and 2025. This is a slight increase (up by 1.6%) from the previous year (4,800).

Over a fifth of people were aged 65 or older (22.2%, or 705,100 people) in 2025. Since 2015, the number of people aged 65 or older has increased by 13.6%. The number of people aged 75 years or older has increased by over a quarter during the same period, up 26.0%. This increased from around 276,400 people in 2015 to around 348,300 people in 2025.

61.0% of the population were aged 16 to 64 years old in 2025, around 1,936,200 people. This number has increased by 1.9% since 2015.

The remaining 16.8% of the population were children and young people aged 0 to 15 (around 533,900). This has decreased by 3.2% since 2015.

## Population by local authority

These estimates are subject to statistical uncertainty, particularly for smaller geographic areas and detailed age-sex breakdowns. The ONS has published research-based measures of statistical uncertainty alongside the estimates, which can be found in the accompanying datasets.

You can use the interactive tool on the ONS website to view the latest population estimates, and measures of statistical uncertainty, for your local area.The population decreased in all but 7 of the 22 local authorities between 2024 and 2025. The largest increases were in:

*   Newport (0.7% increase)
*   Denbighshire (0.4% increase)
*   Monmouthshire (0.2% increase)

The largest decreases were in:

*   Merthyr Tydfil (0.6% decrease)
*   Swansea (0.5% decrease)
*   Neath Port Talbot (0.4% decrease)

Cardiff and Newport were the only local authorities who saw more births than deaths between 2024 and 2025.

7 out of the 22 local authorities saw positive net international migration between 2024 and 2025. 16 out of 22 local authorities saw positive net internal migration.

They comply with the standards of trustworthiness, quality and value in the Code of Practice for Statistics. [On 11 May 2026, the OSR published a compliance check of mid-year population estimates for England and Wales](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/publication/mid-year-population-estimates-for-england-and-wales/).

It is the Welsh Government’s responsibility to maintain compliance with the standards expected of accreditation. If we become concerned about whether these statistics are still meeting the appropriate standards, we will discuss any concerns with OSR promptly. Accreditation can be cancelled or suspended at any point when the highest standards are not maintained, and reinstated when standards are restored.

Accredited official statistics are called National Statistics in the Statistics and Registration Service Act 2007.

### Statement of compliance with the Code of Practice for Statistics

Our statistical practice is regulated by the OSR. OSR sets the standards of trustworthiness, quality and value in the Code of Practice for Statistics that all producers of official statistics should adhere to.

All of our statistics are produced and published in accordance with a number of statements and protocols to enhance trustworthiness, quality and value. These are set out in the Welsh Government’s [Statement of Compliance](https://www.gov.wales/about-statistics-and-research#Statementofcompliance).

These [accredited official statistics (OSR)](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/policies/official-statistics-policies/accredited-official-statistics-policy/) demonstrate the standards expected around trustworthiness, quality and public value in the following ways.

#### Quality

Mid-year estimates of the population are produced by the Office for National statistics. Quality assurance of the population estimates for Wales is performed by Welsh Government statisticians. The statistical bulletin is then drafted, signed off by senior statisticians and published in line with the statement on confidentiality and data access which is informed by the trustworthiness pillar contained in the [Code of Practice for Statistics (UK Statistics Authority)](https://code.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/).

For further information about how these accredited official statistics, published by the ONS, demonstrate the standards expected around trustworthiness, quality and public value, see the [Population estimates for England and Wales quality and methods guide (ONS)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/methodologies/populationestimatesforenglandandwalesqualityandmethodsguide).

You are welcome to contact us directly with any comments about how we meet these standards. Alternatively, you can contact OSR by emailing [regulation@statistics.gov.uk](mailto:regulation@statistics.gov.uk) or via the [OSR website](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/).

### Well-being of Future Generations Act (WFG)

The Well-being of Future Generations Act 2015 is about improving the social, economic, environmental, and cultural wellbeing of Wales. The Act puts in place seven wellbeing goals for Wales. These are for a more equal, prosperous, resilient, healthier, and globally responsible Wales, with cohesive communities and a vibrant culture and thriving Welsh language. Under section (10)(1) of the Act, the Welsh Ministers must (a) publish indicators (“national indicators”) that must be applied for the purpose of measuring progress towards the achievement of the wellbeing goals, and (b) lay a copy of the national indicators before Senedd Cymru. Under section 10(8) of the Well-being of Future Generations Act, where the Welsh Ministers revise the national indicators, they must as soon as reasonably practicable (a) publish the indicators as revised and (b) lay a copy of them before the Senedd. These national indicators were laid before the Senedd in 2021. The indicators laid on 14 December 2021 replace the set laid on 16 March 2016.

Information on the indicators, along with narratives for each of the wellbeing goals and associated technical information is available in the [Wellbeing of Wales report](https://www.gov.wales/wellbeing-wales).

As a national indicator under the Act, they must be referred to in the analyses of local wellbeing produced by public services boards when they are analysing the state of economic, social, environmental, and cultural wellbeing in their areas.

The Act states national milestones must be set that “…the Welsh Ministers consider would assist in measuring whether progress is being made towards the achievement of the wellbeing goals.” In doing so Welsh Ministers must specify how we know that a national milestone has been achieved and the time by which it is to be achieved.

National milestones are not performance targets for any individual organisation but are collective measures of success for Wales.

Some of the national indicators and national milestones use the mid-year estimates of the population as denominators, to calculate rates, for example.

Further information on the [Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015](https://www.gov.wales/well-being-future-generations-wales-act-2015-guidance).

The statistics included in this release could also provide supporting narrative to the national indicators and be used by public services boards in relation to their local wellbeing assessments and local wellbeing plans.

# New mid-year population estimates for England and Wales are here

[![Image 2](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/LI_blog_Data-updates.png)](https://localinsight.org/blog/new-mid-year-population-estimates-for-england-and-wales-are-here/)
**Mid-year population estimates from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) for England & Wales have arrived within Local Insight as both new denominators for various indicators across the site, as well as useful standalone indicators.**

### What are the mid-year estimates?

The mid-year estimates (MYE) aim to represent a population count as of the middle of the year (June 30th). The ONS generates these estimates by taking the most recent Census population snapshot as a starting point and then employs various data sources, such as births, deaths, and migration, to project population changes for subsequent years

Until now, MYE denominators for England and Wales used within the Local Insight platform have been based on the 2011 Census. These new mid-year estimates have been ‘rebased’ using the 2021 Census counts, covering 2021 and 2022, and will now be used as denominators for Local Insight indicators.

You can read more about how the ONS have done the rebasing in [their blog post](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/rebasingofmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowing/rebasingofmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowingcensus2021englandandwales), and their [analysis of this work](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/articles/analysisofrebasedmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowingcensus2021englandandwales/2024-04-09).

There are 1874 indicators that are having their denominators updated in this change, 709 of these are being updated to use 2021 MYE denominators, and 1165 are being updated to use 2022 MYE denominators.

Later in the year, we expect to get 2023 MYE, as well as reworked versions of all mid-year estimates – back to 2011 – adjusted based on the Census 2021 results. These will all be added to Local Insight when they become available.

### How have population figures changed?

Population estimates for most [local authorities have changed by around 5%](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/articles/analysisofrebasedmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowingcensus2021englandandwales/2024-04-09), either positively or negatively, as a result of the rebasing of the ONS mid-year population estimates.

The rebased estimates for England and Wales also increase the female population and decrease the male population for all years. In Wales, however, the decreases to the population estimates for males was larger than those for estimates of females.

### How does this change things on Local Insight?

The shift to the newer MYE data as the denominator has now been implemented for the years 2021 and 2022 for England and Wales. For Scotland, just 2021 MYE data has been added. For indicators with numerators from 2022 or later, the 2022 denominators will be utilised.

**For indicators that have been affected, you may see a few changes:**

*   ******Within time series charts******You’ll be able to see a noticeable change in the percentages in the move from 2020 to 2021 in time series charts. This change is where the previous Census 2021 denominator becomes the new mid-year population estimates, which provides an enhancement in the precision of our rate calculations.

****![Image 3](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Screenshot-2024-04-11-154229.jpg)****

*   ******Within certain indicators******************The side-by-side comparison of Department of Work and Pensions indicators below shows how some indicators on Local Insight are being affected by this change.There is a large change for Westminster, which was identified by the ONS as having one of the highest percentage differences between the older rolled-forward mid-year population estimates and the newly rebased population estimates for 2021.![Image 4](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/MYE-example-1024x532.png)Another example of where there might be larger differences is in areas with a high Unattributable Population Change (UPC) – which is defined as a change to population estimates that can’t be explained by the ONS components of change. Large cities with a significant student population, like Coventry, are more likely to have high UPC – as are areas with a large proportion of young, mobile residents. This is because previous rounds of MYE spread the UPC evenly across all age groups. The new approach recognises that unexplained population changes are typically concentrated among certain age groups that are more transient, rather than being evenly distributed. As a result, areas with larger young adult populations are now seeing bigger adjustments in their population estimates compared to the previous method. The ONS [explores this within their blog](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/rebasingofmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowing/rebasingofmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowingcensus2021englandandwales).

### Which new indicators have been added?

MYE indicators have been added to England and Wales Local Insight within the following topics: 5-year bands from 0-5 up to 85-90+, total population, population density and broader grouping (for example 0-65 and 0-19).

For the full list of [new indicators, download this spreadsheet.](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/MYE_2022.csv)[Right click and ‘Save link as…’ to download]

### Viewing these indicators on the Map

These indicators are not assigned to a theme and will need to be added to a theme to be viewable on the map. For assistance in doing this, we recommend taking a look at the Help Centre article [on adding new indicators to your themes.](https://support.localinsight.org/en/articles/270653-adding-a-new-indicator-to-a-theme)_[Subscription only access]_

![Image 5](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Screenshot-2024-04-15-112816.png)

### Viewing these indicators on the Dashboard

These indicators can be viewed on the dashboard for all your custom areas: s imply navigate to the dashboard, click Data and Custom Dashboard. You can then [search](https://support.localinsight.org/en/articles/254769-build-a-dashboard)_[Subscription only access]_ for the indicators using their names.

![Image 6](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Screenshot-2024-04-15-121033-1024x250.png)

### **FAQs**

**Which population indicators do you recommend are used? The count from the 2021 Census, or these new mid-year estimates?**

Whilst there are likely still situations where the Census 2021 population figures may be better suited, generally we would say that the Mid Year Estimates (MYE) are recommended for a more up-to-date picture of the population in your area.

To clarify, the MYE takes the census estimates as a starting point and rolls them forward based on information regarding births, deaths and administrative data on internal and international migration. This is also why we have made it a priority to implement them as denominators for various Local Insight indicators so shortly after their release. They are considered particularly reliable at Local Authority geography levels and above but be aware they are progressively less so for smaller areas.

**Why are the 2021 Census population indicators still being used in Reports, and when will the MYE indicators be used?**

This update has laid the groundwork for a second stage of MYE updates, where we intend to include the MYE in Reports. This will happen when the backdated MYE data becomes available (for 2011 to 2020) so that we can show how an area’s population is changing in time series charts. We will also update older MYE denominators with this data.

We expect this data to be made available over the next few months, as well as further Scottish MYE data, and 2023 data. At this point we will also replace the relevant Census 2021 population figures with the most recent MYE data – which we expect to be the 2023 MYE. These decisions have been made to strike the balance of giving Local Insight users new data as soon as possible but also to manage the staggered release of MYE data from the ONS in a consistent way across the site.

# New mid-year population estimates for England and Wales are here

[![Image 2](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/LI_blog_Data-updates.png)](https://localinsight.org/blog/new-mid-year-population-estimates-for-england-and-wales-are-here/)
**Mid-year population estimates from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) for England & Wales have arrived within Local Insight as both new denominators for various indicators across the site, as well as useful standalone indicators.**

### What are the mid-year estimates?

The mid-year estimates (MYE) aim to represent a population count as of the middle of the year (June 30th). The ONS generates these estimates by taking the most recent Census population snapshot as a starting point and then employs various data sources, such as births, deaths, and migration, to project population changes for subsequent years

Until now, MYE denominators for England and Wales used within the Local Insight platform have been based on the 2011 Census. These new mid-year estimates have been ‘rebased’ using the 2021 Census counts, covering 2021 and 2022, and will now be used as denominators for Local Insight indicators.

You can read more about how the ONS have done the rebasing in [their blog post](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/rebasingofmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowing/rebasingofmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowingcensus2021englandandwales), and their [analysis of this work](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/articles/analysisofrebasedmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowingcensus2021englandandwales/2024-04-09).

There are 1874 indicators that are having their denominators updated in this change, 709 of these are being updated to use 2021 MYE denominators, and 1165 are being updated to use 2022 MYE denominators.

Later in the year, we expect to get 2023 MYE, as well as reworked versions of all mid-year estimates – back to 2011 – adjusted based on the Census 2021 results. These will all be added to Local Insight when they become available.

### How have population figures changed?

Population estimates for most [local authorities have changed by around 5%](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/articles/analysisofrebasedmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowingcensus2021englandandwales/2024-04-09), either positively or negatively, as a result of the rebasing of the ONS mid-year population estimates.

The rebased estimates for England and Wales also increase the female population and decrease the male population for all years. In Wales, however, the decreases to the population estimates for males was larger than those for estimates of females.

### How does this change things on Local Insight?

The shift to the newer MYE data as the denominator has now been implemented for the years 2021 and 2022 for England and Wales. For Scotland, just 2021 MYE data has been added. For indicators with numerators from 2022 or later, the 2022 denominators will be utilised.

**For indicators that have been affected, you may see a few changes:**

*   ******Within time series charts******You’ll be able to see a noticeable change in the percentages in the move from 2020 to 2021 in time series charts. This change is where the previous Census 2021 denominator becomes the new mid-year population estimates, which provides an enhancement in the precision of our rate calculations.

****![Image 3](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Screenshot-2024-04-11-154229.jpg)****

*   ******Within certain indicators******************The side-by-side comparison of Department of Work and Pensions indicators below shows how some indicators on Local Insight are being affected by this change.There is a large change for Westminster, which was identified by the ONS as having one of the highest percentage differences between the older rolled-forward mid-year population estimates and the newly rebased population estimates for 2021.![Image 4](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/MYE-example-1024x532.png)Another example of where there might be larger differences is in areas with a high Unattributable Population Change (UPC) – which is defined as a change to population estimates that can’t be explained by the ONS components of change. Large cities with a significant student population, like Coventry, are more likely to have high UPC – as are areas with a large proportion of young, mobile residents. This is because previous rounds of MYE spread the UPC evenly across all age groups. The new approach recognises that unexplained population changes are typically concentrated among certain age groups that are more transient, rather than being evenly distributed. As a result, areas with larger young adult populations are now seeing bigger adjustments in their population estimates compared to the previous method. The ONS [explores this within their blog](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/bulletins/rebasingofmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowing/rebasingofmidyearpopulationestimatesfollowingcensus2021englandandwales).

### Which new indicators have been added?

MYE indicators have been added to England and Wales Local Insight within the following topics: 5-year bands from 0-5 up to 85-90+, total population, population density and broader grouping (for example 0-65 and 0-19).

For the full list of [new indicators, download this spreadsheet.](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/MYE_2022.csv)[Right click and ‘Save link as…’ to download]

### Viewing these indicators on the Map

These indicators are not assigned to a theme and will need to be added to a theme to be viewable on the map. For assistance in doing this, we recommend taking a look at the Help Centre article [on adding new indicators to your themes.](https://support.localinsight.org/en/articles/270653-adding-a-new-indicator-to-a-theme)_[Subscription only access]_

![Image 5](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Screenshot-2024-04-15-112816.png)

### Viewing these indicators on the Dashboard

These indicators can be viewed on the dashboard for all your custom areas: s imply navigate to the dashboard, click Data and Custom Dashboard. You can then [search](https://support.localinsight.org/en/articles/254769-build-a-dashboard)_[Subscription only access]_ for the indicators using their names.

![Image 6](https://localinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Screenshot-2024-04-15-121033-1024x250.png)

### **FAQs**

**Which population indicators do you recommend are used? The count from the 2021 Census, or these new mid-year estimates?**

Whilst there are likely still situations where the Census 2021 population figures may be better suited, generally we would say that the Mid Year Estimates (MYE) are recommended for a more up-to-date picture of the population in your area.

To clarify, the MYE takes the census estimates as a starting point and rolls them forward based on information regarding births, deaths and administrative data on internal and international migration. This is also why we have made it a priority to implement them as denominators for various Local Insight indicators so shortly after their release. They are considered particularly reliable at Local Authority geography levels and above but be aware they are progressively less so for smaller areas.

**Why are the 2021 Census population indicators still being used in Reports, and when will the MYE indicators be used?**

This update has laid the groundwork for a second stage of MYE updates, where we intend to include the MYE in Reports. This will happen when the backdated MYE data becomes available (for 2011 to 2020) so that we can show how an area’s population is changing in time series charts. We will also update older MYE denominators with this data.

We expect this data to be made available over the next few months, as well as further Scottish MYE data, and 2023 data. At this point we will also replace the relevant Census 2021 population figures with the most recent MYE data – which we expect to be the 2023 MYE. These decisions have been made to strike the balance of giving Local Insight users new data as soon as possible but also to manage the staggered release of MYE data from the ONS in a consistent way across the site.

## About this dataset

 The midyear (30 June) estimates of population are based on results from the latest Census of Population with allowance for under-enumeration. Available at Local Authority level and above. 
_Rebasing of population estimates:_ This dataset contains the population estimates for each country and local authority of the UK rebased to the results of the 2021/2022 censuses across the UK. These estimates replace previously published estimates for 2011 to 2022.

_Usual residence definitions:_ the estimated resident population of an area includes all those people who usually live there, regardless of nationality. Arriving international migrants are included in the usually resident population if they remain in the UK for at least a year. Emigrants are excluded if they remain outside the UK for at least a year. This is consistent with the United Nations definition of a long-term migrant. Armed forces stationed outside of the UK are excluded. Students are taken to be usually resident at their term time address.

# Population projections

Projections of the future size and age structure of the population of the UK and its constituent countries. Based on mid-year population estimates and assumptions of future fertility, mortality and migration.

## On this page:

*   Dataset
*   Publications

## View all content related to this topic:

## Spotlight

![Image 3](https://cdn.ons.gov.uk/assets/images/latest-publications.png)

### [National population projections: 2024-based](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/bulletins/nationalpopulationprojections/2024based)

#### What's in the bulletin?

*   The UK population is projected to reach 71 million by 2034.
*   This is slower growth than our previous, 2022-based projections, which projected the UK population would reach 72.2 million by mid-2034.
*   Over the first 10 years of our projections period, the population is projected to grow from 69.3 million in mid-2024 to 71.0 million in mid-2034, an increase of 1.7 million (2.5%); the increase arises from net international migration. 

Read this statistical bulletin

### [Subnational population projections for England: 2022-based](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/bulletins/subnationalpopulationprojectionsforengland/2022based)

#### What's in the bulletin?

*   The population of England is projected to increase by 6.4% between mid-2022 and mid-2032 compared with 5.9% for the UK.
*   Between mid-2022 and mid-2032 the population is projected to increase across all regions as well as in 302 of the 309 local authorities in England (based on 2021 boundaries).
*   Tower Hamlets is projected to be the fastest growing local authority between mid-2022 and mid-2032, with a 20.4% projected population increase (excludes the City of London).

## Datasets related to Population projections

*   ### [2020-based interim national population projections: year ending June 2022 estimated international migration variant](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/datasets/2020basedinterimnationalpopulationprojectionsyearendingjune2022estimatedinternationalmigrationvariant)

2020-based interim national population projections with assumptions of possible future international migration that reflect estimates of international migration to year ending June 2022. These statistics are widely used in planning, for example, fiscal projections, health, education and pensions. Not national statistics.

*   ### [Principal projection - UK summary](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/datasets/tablea11principalprojectionuksummary)

Principal projection for the UK including population by broad age group, components of change and summary statistics.

Machine-readable data for United Kingdom principal and variant projections. Single year of age and sex with underlying data. 
*   ### [Population projections for regions by five-year age groups and sex, England](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/datasets/regionsinenglandtable1)

*   ### [Population projections for local authorities by five-year age groups and sex, England](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/datasets/localauthoritiesinenglandtable2)

Population figures over a 25-year period, by five-year age groups and sex for local authorities in England. 2022-based datasets are the latest projection.

## Publications related to Population projections

### Statistical bulletins

*   #### [National population projections: 2024-based](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/bulletins/nationalpopulationprojections/2024based)

The potential future population size of the UK and its constituent countries. These statistics are widely used in planning, including fiscal projections, health, education and pensions.

*   #### [Subnational population projections for England: 2022-based](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/bulletins/subnationalpopulationprojectionsforengland/2022based)

Population projections by English local authorities and health geographies. These statistics are used in planning, health and education.

*   #### [Household projections for England: 2022-based](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/bulletins/householdprojectionsforengland/2022based)

Household projections give an indication of the future number of households in England and its regions and local authorities. Used for planning in areas such as housing and social care.

*   #### [Variant subnational population projections for England: 2016-based](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/bulletins/variantsubnationalpopulationprojectionsforengland/2016based)

2016-based variant subnational population projections, including a variant based on a 10-year trend of migration data and variants with higher and lower levels of net international migration.

An update on the recent invitation to users to provide feedback on the future timescales for national and subnational population projections for the UK.

# Population projections

Projections of the future size and age structure of the population of the UK and its constituent countries. Based on mid-year population estimates and assumptions of future fertility, mortality and migration.

## On this page:

### [National population projections: 2024-based](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/bulletins/nationalpopulationprojections/2024based)

#### What's in the bulletin?

*   The UK population is projected to reach 71 million by 2034.
*   This is slower growth than our previous, 2022-based projections, which projected the UK population would reach 72.2 million by mid-2034.
*   Over the first 10 years of our projections period, the population is projected to grow from 69.3 million in mid-2024 to 71.0 million in mid-2034, an increase of 1.7 million (2.5%); the increase arises from net international migration.

### [Subnational population projections for England: 2022-based](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationprojections/bulletins/subnationalpopulationprojectionsforengland/2022based)

#### What's in the bulletin?

*   The population of England is projected to increase by 6.4% between mid-2022 and mid-2032 compared with 5.9% for the UK.
*   Between mid-2022 and mid-2032 the population is projected to increase across all regions as well as in 302 of the 309 local authorities in England (based on 2021 boundaries).
*   Tower Hamlets is projected to be the fastest growing local authority between mid-2022 and mid-2032, with a 20.4% projected population increase (excludes the City of London).

### ONS’s decision to continue with its current methods

On 4 March, ONS announced that it no longer plans to move to the ABPEs in summer 2026 and will instead focus on continuous improvement activity for the MYEs. ONS’s transparent communication of the decision, using the criteria[recommended by OSR](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/publication/admin-based-population-estimates-for-england-and-wales/pages/3/), demonstrated a clear commitment to support user understanding and confidence in its decision-making processes.

The decision to continue with the MYEs as the official headline population estimates is a significant pivot away from ONS’s previous ambition to make the ABPEs the official headline measure. As outlined[in our response letter](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/correspondence/ed-humpherson-to-mary-gregory-response-to-ons-plans-for-mid-year-population-estimates/), the announcement highlighted important areas for improvement within the current system, such as for the methods used to estimate internal migration and disaggregate long-term international migration at a local authority level.

These known limitations with the current methods (described in more detail in the section on[user confidence in subnational and sub-population](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/publication/mid-year-population-estimates-for-england-and-wales/pages/4/#_User_confidence_in)) may lead some users to question the continued reliance on existing methods. It is therefore important that ONS clarifies the strengths and limitations of the methods and develops new strategic goals and objectives to help drive the work forward.

Requirement 1: To support user confidence in its decision to continue with the MYEs, ONS must be open and explicit about the strengths and limitations of the current methods and what action ONS is taking, with time scales, to address methodological limitations with independent assurance.

ONS is currently hosting internal workshops to develop revised research plans for alternative approaches to population estimates, drawing on the insight gleaned from the development of the ABPEs and planned improvements to internal migration and the disaggregation of international migration. Publishing these revised plans, which are clearly aligned to ONS’s goals and objectives, will help ensure users remain well informed in an open and transparent way.
